short.headline: India’s water crisis is underground and agricultural, not in city taps
short.dek: National groundwater extraction looks safe at 60%, but in Punjab it’s 156%. Meanwhile, tap-water access surges. Here’s the data.
short.body: India’s water stress is often misunderstood. Per-capita water availability has fallen from 1,816 cubic metres in 2001 to a projected 1,367 in 2031, crossing the water‑stress threshold. Yet the national average hides a deeper crisis: in the northwest farming belt, groundwater is being mined far faster than it can recharge. Agriculture takes 90% of all freshwater. While the resource shrinks, drinking‑water access has improved markedly, 76% of Indians now have safely managed water. This page unpacks the numbers.

macha.heading: Okay, but what does this actually mean, macha?
macha.body: The water crisis isn’t about your tap running dry tomorrow—it’s about what’s happening silently under the wheat fields of Punjab, Rajasthan and Haryana. Those states are pumping out groundwater at over 150% of what the rains put back. Imagine a bank account where you withdraw more than you deposit every year. That’s those aquifers. Meanwhile, most of India is okay, and the government has done a genuinely big thing: it got tap water to eight out of ten rural homes in five years. So the story is not that India is about to run out of water. It is that we are spending our water savings much too fast in a few places where our food comes from, and we haven’t fixed that yet.
macha.soWhat: We’re getting better at giving people water at home, but the underground reserve that fills those taps is being emptied where it matters most.

article.title: Water Stress in India: What the Data Says
article.standfirst: India pumps a quarter of the world’s groundwater, mostly for farms. National data says it’s using 60% of what refills, but drill down and the northwest is mining water at over 150%. Tap water has reached 80% of rural homes. Here’s the full picture, number by number.
article.bodyMarkdown:
## How much water does India have per person, and is it falling?

In 2001, India had an average annual per‑capita water availability of 1,816 cubic metres per person per year. By 2031, that figure is projected to fall to 1,367 cubic metres. This number comes from dividing the country’s total renewable water resource by its population. A widely used benchmark, the Falkenmark indicator, calls a nation ‘water‑stressed’ when availability drops below 1,700 cubic metres per person per year, and ‘water‑scarce’ when it falls below 1,000. India crossed the stress line some time ago and is now edging toward scarcity. The decline is almost entirely driven by population growth, not a shrinking water resource. The total amount of water that flows through India each year has not changed much, but each person’s share gets smaller as the country grows.

## How much of India’s water can actually be used?

A common headline number says India has 1,999 billion cubic metres of water each year. Most of that cannot be captured. When the monsoon rains fall, a large share rushes out to sea. The country’s storage and extraction capacity means only a portion is actually available. The utilizable water is estimated at 1,137 billion cubic metres per year, made up of 690 billion cubic metres of surface water that can be stored and 447 billion cubic metres of replenishable groundwater. Whenever someone quotes the larger figure as if it were India’s usable supply, they are misleading you. The real ceiling for all human uses is about half of that.

## At the national level, is India pumping groundwater sustainably?

The single metric used to track groundwater health is the stage of extraction: total groundwater pumped each year divided by the annual extractable resource. A figure below 100% means the aquifer is getting back at least as much as is taken out. Above 100%, it is being mined. For India as a whole, the stage of extraction in 2025 is 60.6%, down slightly from 61.6% in 2020. This national number has hovered around 60% for several years, which officials often present as proof that groundwater is under control. It is not that simple. A national average is a blanket that hides what is happening underneath.

## What do local assessments reveal about groundwater stress?

The Central Ground Water Board divides the country into 6,762 small assessment units, blocks, talukas and mandals, and classifies each based on its stage of extraction. Of these, 4,949 units (73.16%) are ‘safe’, meaning extraction is less than 70% of the rechargeable amount. Another 758 (11.2%) are ‘semi‑critical’. But 201 units (2.97%) are ‘critical’ and 730 units (10.79%) are ‘over‑exploited’, pumping out more than nature puts back. An additional 127 units are classified saline, where the water is naturally unfit for use. So about one in nine assessment units is already in the red. These over‑exploited pockets are not empty patches on a map; they hold large populations and productive farmland. The national average, with its calm 60%, is a smoothed‑out picture that erases this local damage.

## Where is groundwater depletion worst in India?

Put the state‑level extraction numbers on a map and the abstraction turns into a sharp regional emergency. Punjab tops the list with a stage of extraction of 156.4%. Rajasthan follows at 147.1% and Haryana at 136.8%. Delhi, a city‑state with a huge population, extracts 92.1% of its renewable groundwater each year. Together, these states form a contiguous belt in the northwest, India’s grain bowl. The rest of the country looks very different. Tamil Nadu, for instance, shows 73.5%, which is high but still within recharge limits, and its hard‑rock aquifers behave differently from the thick alluvial sediments of the north. The crisis has a clear address: the Indo‑Gangetic plains of Punjab, Haryana and western Rajasthan.

## How have groundwater levels changed in the worst‑hit states?

A look at the trend from 2020 to 2025 shows that the worst states have not moved below 100%. The national line stays flat at around 60‑61%. Punjab’s extraction has eased from 164.4% to 156.4%, but the state still takes more than one and a half times what is recharged. Haryana’s figure has actually crept up from 134.6% to 136.8%. Rajasthan dropped from 150.2% to 147.1%. Delhi fell from 101.4% to 92.1%, technically dipping below the over‑exploitation line, though it remains under severe stress. Tamil Nadu improved from 82.9% to 73.5%. These small declines are not a recovery. Extraction that is 30 or 50 percentage points above 100% year after year means the water table is still falling. The savings account is still being emptied, just a little less quickly in some places.

## Which sectors consume India’s water?

Any serious conversation about water must start with the question: who is using it? In India, the answer is farmland. Agriculture takes 90.4% of all freshwater withdrawals. Households use just 7.4%, and industry a tiny 2.2%. These are the latest FAO AQUASTAT modelled estimates, carried forward to 2022. The picture has barely changed in decades: in 1975 farming was 93% of the total, domestic use was 3%. So the image of a city running dry is emotionally powerful, but it is not where the real volume goes. India’s water problem is, fundamentally, a farming problem. Any solution that does not work through the agricultural sector will only nibble at the edges.

## How efficiently does India use its water?

Water productivity measures how much economic output a country squeezes out of each cubic metre of freshwater it withdraws. India’s water productivity has climbed from $0.61 per cubic metre (constant 2015 US dollars) in 1975 to $4.62 in 2022. That is a large percentage rise, but the absolute level remains low compared with industrialised economies. Much of the increase reflects not a sudden improvement in irrigation technique but the economy gradually shifting toward services, which use very little water per rupee of output. The number also tells us that a very large volume of water is tied up in a sector that produces a relatively small share of the country’s total income. India earns very little per drop because most of that drop waters a wheat or rice field.

## How safe is India’s remaining groundwater for drinking?

Quantity is only half the story. The groundwater that remains is often unfit to drink. In 2024, the Central Ground Water Board tested samples from 15,259 monitoring sites across the country. Nitrate exceeded the safe limit of 45 mg/L in 19.8% of those samples. Fluoride was above 1.5 mg/L in 9% of samples, and arsenic crossed the 10 ppb threshold in 3.1% of samples. These are nationwide averages; the contamination is concentrated in known problem pockets, so in those areas the effective share is far higher. The data is a reminder that even where water is physically present, it may carry a health cost that is invisible until a child falls ill or a patch of skin begins to discolour.

## Where are groundwater contamination hotspots in India?

Natural contaminants do not respect district boundaries, but they do cluster in patterns. Nitrate affects parts of 443 districts across 23 states and union territories, making it the most widespread contaminant. Fluoride appears in parts of 263 districts across 20 states and union territories. Uranium, which is increasingly discussed as the next big quality challenge, is found in parts of 132 districts in 13 states and union territories. Arsenic, the contaminant that made the Bengal delta a global public‑health case study, is present in parts of 118 districts across 20 states and union territories. The phrase ‘parts of’ matters: a district listed here does not mean every well in it is unsafe. It means that testing found exceedances in specific locations, often tied to local geology or agricultural run‑off.

## Has access to tap water improved in rural India?

In 2019, only 16.7% of rural households had a tap‑water connection. By 2025, under the Jal Jeevan Mission, that share had jumped to 79.7%. This is one of the fastest infrastructure roll‑outs in the country’s history. But the number is self‑reported by the agencies providing the connections, and the Comptroller and Auditor General has flagged gaps between connections counted and taps that actually deliver water reliably. Functionality is not the same as registration. Still, the direction is unmistakable. For a rural family that once walked to a public standpost, a tap at home changes the texture of daily life, even if it runs only a few hours a day.

## How many Indians have safely managed drinking water today?

The World Health Organization and UNICEF track drinking water access through a stricter lens: safely managed water must be on the premises, available when needed, and free of contamination. Using that definition, India has moved from 37.6% of the population in 2000 to 76.4% in 2024. That is a genuine public‑health success. The metric does not, however, ask whether the aquifer that supplies the pipe is stable. It is a measure of the service arriving at the household, not of the resource behind it. So it can rise fast even as the water table falls.

## How can water access improve while freshwater per person falls?

India’s renewable internal freshwater resources per person have collapsed from 3,238 cubic metres in 1961 to 1,014 cubic metres in 2022. Over the same broad period, the share of people with safely managed drinking water more than doubled. The two lines move in opposite directions because they measure wildly different things. The per‑capita figure divides the country’s total internal water resource by its population; it is a physical endowment indicator, and most of that water is not for households but for agriculture. The drinking‑water metric counts pipes and taps. One can rise while the other falls. The paradox is that India is getting better at delivering water to people at the very moment the source it draws from is being depleted in its most productive agricultural heartland. That is not a contradiction, it is a warning.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: Think of a well as a bank account. Each year the rain tops it up with a certain amount of water—that’s the recharge. The share you can safely withdraw is the extractable resource. Stage of extraction is simply how much you are actually taking out divided by that safe amount, shown as a percentage. Below 100% means you are living within the account’s means; above 100% means you are dipping into the capital, and one day it will be empty. It is the single most important number on this page.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: The national figure of 60.6% suggests India is safe, but drill down to state and block level and the story flips. Punjab is at 156%, mining its reserves. That is why the stage of extraction must be read at the local scale, never just the national average.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: A simple rule of thumb used around the world. If a country has less than 1,700 cubic metres of renewable freshwater per person per year, it is considered water‑stressed. Below 1,000, it is water‑scarce. It is like a household budget: above a certain line you can cover your basics, but below it you start making hard choices. The threshold is not about actual consumption but about the resource available to share.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: India’s per‑capita water availability has fallen from 1,816 m³ in 2001 to a projected 1,367 m³ in 2031, crossing straight through the stress line. The Falkenmark number gives a name to what that downward graph means: the country is now officially water‑stressed, and if the trend continues, it will approach scarcity.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: To understand groundwater, the Central Ground Water Board does not look at India as one big lump. It slices the country into thousands of small pieces—blocks, talukas and mandals. Each of these is an assessment unit, a localised area where the balance of rain, pumping and geology can be measured. Classifying them as Safe, Semi‑Critical, Critical or Over‑Exploited tells you exactly where the pressure is building.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: The national average says groundwater use is 60.6%, which sounds okay. But when you look unit by unit, you find 730 of them over‑exploited. Those units are not empty deserts; they support millions of people. The assessment units are where the average breaks down and the real pain shows.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: Imagine a heavy downpour. Much of the water rushes off the roof, down the drain and is lost. The amount you actually capture in a tank is your utilizable water. For a country, the total annual rainfall that flows through rivers and into the ground is the resource, but only the portion that can be stored behind dams or extracted from wells is utilizable. The rest flows out to sea.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: India’s total water resource is often quoted as 1,999 billion cubic metres per year, but the utilizable share is only 1,137 billion cubic metres. Every policy that treats the bigger number as available supply is building on sand.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: Water productivity is a measure of how much economic value a country creates from each cubic metre of freshwater it uses. It is calculated as GDP divided by total freshwater withdrawal. A high number means the country earns more money for every drop; a low number means a lot of water is going into activities that create relatively little income. It is not just about efficiency—it also reflects what kind of economy a country has.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: India’s water productivity has risen from $0.61 to $4.62 per cubic metre, but it remains low by global standards because 90% of water goes to agriculture. The rise partly comes from the economy shifting to services, not from farms using less water. That matters when you think about who should be paying the real cost of water.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: This is a high bar set by the World Health Organization and UNICEF. It means drinking water that is available on your premises, comes out of a tap or a protected source, is there when you need it, and is free of faecal and chemical contamination. It is not just a connection; it is a guarantee that every glass is safe.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: India has pushed this figure from 37.6% to 76.4% in two decades. That is genuine progress. But note what it does not measure: it says nothing about whether the aquifer supplying that tap is sustainable. So the chart can rise while the groundwater table falls, and that is exactly the paradox playing out on this page.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: A flagship central government programme launched to provide a functional tap‑water connection to every rural household. It tracks coverage as the percentage of households that have been given a connection. The number is self‑reported by implementing agencies, and the Comptroller and Auditor General has pointed out that a connection is not the same as a tap that actually runs.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: The programme took rural tap coverage from 16.7% in 2019 to 79.7% in 2025. That is a staggering speed, but the reader should hold two thoughts at once: many more homes now have a tap, and the water behind that tap is often being pumped unsustainably.

chartExplainers.title: India keeps slipping down the water ladder
chartExplainers.takeaway: Per‑capita water availability fell from 1,816 m³ in 2001 to a projected 1,367 m³ in 2031, crossing below the water‑stress threshold of 1,700 m³.
chartExplainers.detail: This line chart tracks the average annual volume of renewable water available per person each year. The resource itself has not shrunk dramatically; the line falls because India’s population has grown from about 1 billion in 2001 to a projected 1.5 billion in 2031. The Falkenmark benchmark calls a country water‑stressed below 1,700 m³ per person per year and water‑scarce below 1,000 m³. India has passed the stress mark and is approaching scarcity. The 2031 figure is a projection, not a measurement, so it assumes the population continues to grow while the water resource stays roughly the same. That is a reasonable but not guaranteed assumption.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: The simplest measure of stress: how much water there is to go round, per person, as the population keeps growing.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Follow the line downwards. The key points are the start (1,816 m³ in 2001) and the projected end (1,367 m³ in 2031). The big drop in between is the population effect.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not confuse this with actual water withdrawals or consumption; it’s a resource availability metric based on average rainfall.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: The line is sparse with large labels; the decline is clear even on a small screen.

chartExplainers.title: How much of India’s water can actually be used
chartExplainers.takeaway: Only 1,137 billion cubic metres of India’s 1,999 billion cubic metres annual water resource is utilizable.
chartExplainers.detail: The chart shows the total average annual water resource (1,999 BCM), the total utilizable water (1,137 BCM), and its two components: utilizable surface water (690 BCM) and replenishable groundwater (447 BCM). The gap between the total and the utilizable figure is the water that flows out to sea during monsoons or cannot be captured with existing infrastructure. When a minister says India has plenty of water, they are almost always citing the 1,999 BCM figure. That is not false, but it is misleading, it is like counting the rain that falls on your roof as what reaches your tank.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: The ‘headline number’ hides that most water cannot be stored or extracted, so it corrects a common misrepresentation.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Compare the lengths of the horizontal bars. The top bar (total resource) is nearly twice the length of the second bar (utilizable). The two smaller bars show how the utilizable share splits.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not cite the total resource as available supply; only the utilizable portion can be managed.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Horizontal bars render well on any screen, and the difference in magnitude is instantly visible.

chartExplainers.title: Nationally, India pumps about 60% of what refills each year

chartExplainers.title: Most blocks are safe – but one in nine is over‑exploited
chartExplainers.takeaway: Of 6,762 assessment units, 4,949 are safe and 730 are over‑exploited, that is one in nine.
chartExplainers.detail: The bar chart breaks the country into its assessment units, small administrative areas where groundwater can be locally measured. chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Breaking the country into thousands of small assessment units shows the damage the national average buries.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Look at the Over‑Exploited bar and compare it to the Safe bar. The length difference is large, but the Over‑Exploited bar is not negligible.

chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Water stress is also an efficiency story: how much economic value India wrings from each unit of water.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Watch the rising line. The upward slope is good, but the absolute value is what matters; $4.62 per m³ is still low, showing that most water goes to low‑value uses.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not credit agriculture with the rise; much of the gain comes from India’s shift to services.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: A clean single line with clear dollar labels works nicely on mobile.

chartExplainers.title: The water that is left is often unsafe
chartExplainers.takeaway: 19.8% of tested groundwater samples exceed the safe limit for nitrate, 9% for fluoride and 3.1% for arsenic.
chartExplainers.detail: The horizontal bars display the share of monitoring sites where a contaminant exceeded the health‑based guideline value. Nitrate is the most common, at 19.8% of the 15,259 sites tested in 2024. Fluoride is next at 9%, concentrated in parts of Rajasthan, Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh. Arsenic is at 3.1%, largely in the Ganga‑Brahmaputra plains. These are measured exceedances. The real picture in unmonitored wells, especially private agricultural borewells that are never tested, could be worse. The chart is a reminder that quantity and quality are linked. As water tables drop, concentrations of natural contaminants can rise.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Depletion is only half the problem, what remains is increasingly contaminated.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Each bar is the percentage of tested sites above the safe limit. The nitrate bar is about twice as long as the fluoride bar.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: These are from monitored sites only; contamination may be worse in unmonitored areas.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Three horizontal bars with clear labels are ideal for mobile; no clutter, just the numbers.

chartExplainers.title: Contamination reaches into hundreds of districts
chartExplainers.takeaway: Nitrate is found in parts of 443 districts, fluoride in 263, uranium in 132 and arsenic in 118.
chartExplainers.detail: This bar chart maps the geographic spread of the four key contaminants. Nitrate, largely from fertiliser run‑off and waste, touches parts of 443 districts across 23 states and union territories, more than half the country’s districts. Fluoride appears in 263 districts across 20 states/UTs. Uranium, a naturally occurring heavy metal, is recorded in 132 districts across 13 states/UTs, and arsenic in 118 districts across 20 states/UTs. The phrase ‘parts of’ is critical: a district counted here does not mean every block in the district drinks contaminated water. It means testing found exceedances somewhere within its borders. The widespread nature of these findings, however, shows that water quality is not a localised problem; it is a national public‑health challenge.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Quality problems are not a few isolated villages, they are spread across much of the country.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Compare bar lengths. The nitrate bar is the longest; it represents over 400 districts. The others are shorter but still large.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: ‘Parts of’ means contamination is localised within districts, not that the entire district is unsafe.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Horizontal bars with district counts are simple to parse; the note about ‘parts of’ must be clearly stated.

chartExplainers.title: Tap water reached most of rural India in five years
chartExplainers.takeaway: Rural household tap‑water coverage jumped from 16.7% in 2019 to 79.7% in 2025 under the Jal Jeevan Mission.
chartExplainers.detail: The line chart shows a near‑vertical rise. In 2019, only 16.7% of rural homes had a tap. By 2025, the Jal Jeevan Mission dashboard reported 79.7% coverage. This is one of the fastest infrastructure expansions in Indian history. The number is self‑reported by implementing agencies, and audits by the Comptroller and Auditor General have flagged gaps between connections counted and taps that actually deliver drinking water every day. The number therefore is best read as reported coverage, not a guarantee that every listed household receives a reliable supply. Yet the direction of change is real. A tap at home, even if it runs for a few hours, replaces a long daily walk to a standpost.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: The state’s biggest recent water success, and the human counterpoint to the depletion story.
chartExplainers.howToRead: The line shoots upward from left to right. The steepness is the story.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not equate a connection with reliable, potable supply; CAG audits have found functionality gaps.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: A single rising line is one of the most mobile‑friendly charts; just one number to track.

chartExplainers.title: Safe drinking water finally reaches most homes
chartExplainers.takeaway: The share of the population using safely managed drinking water rose from 37.6% in 2000 to 76.4% in 2024.
chartExplainers.detail: This line charts the WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme’s strict metric of drinking‑water service. ‘Safely managed’ means water on premises, available when needed and free of contamination. India doubled this number over two decades. The rise was gradual before 2015 and accelerated in recent years, coinciding with large central schemes. Unlike the tap‑connection count, this metric is independently estimated and reflects what households actually report. The caveat is that it does not reflect the sustainability of the water source. A household can have safe drinking water today while the aquifer that supplies it is being drained. That tension runs through the entire page.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: The genuine good‑news counterpoint: access has improved markedly.
chartExplainers.howToRead: The line climbs steadily from bottom left to top right. The latest value, 76.4%, is the headline.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: This metric does not measure water source sustainability; it can rise even as groundwater levels fall.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: A smooth upward line with a clear endpoint is easy to grasp on a phone.

chartExplainers.title: More taps, less water: the paradox in one frame
chartExplainers.takeaway: As safe drinking water access climbed to 76%, renewable freshwater per person fell to 1,014 cubic metres.
chartExplainers.detail: This dual‑axis chart pairs two lines that move in opposite directions. The first line shows the rise in safely managed drinking water, from 37.6% in 2000 to 76.4% in 2024. The second line tracks renewable internal freshwater resources per person, which dropped from 3,238 m³ in 1961 to 1,014 m³ in 2022. They are different units, so the dual axes keep them from being directly compared, but the trend conflict is the point. One line is about the pipes reaching homes; the other is about the total water that exists in rivers and aquifers per person. India is getting better at delivery while the underlying resource per head shrinks. The gain in access is real and vital, but it rests on a foundation that is being hollowed out in the very regions that feed the country.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: The article’s thesis: India is getting better at delivering water to people while the resource itself shrinks.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Look at the two y‑axes. One is percentage, the other is cubic metres. The rising line is access; the falling line is resource per person.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not treat the lines as directly comparable units; one is a service delivery metric, the other a physical resource average.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Dual‑axis charts need clear labels for each axis and a note to read them separately; on mobile, keep the design simple.

editorialPlanDraft.answerThesis: India's water stress is most severe in its northwest agricultural belt, where groundwater extraction far exceeds recharge, while national averages obscure the crisis and drinking-water access improves even as per-capita water availability declines.
requiredConcepts: Stage of groundwater extraction: annual groundwater extraction divided by the annual extractable (replenishable) resource, as a percentage; below 100% the aquifer is refilling at least as fast as it is pumped, above 100% it is being mined and cannot last; this is the single most important number on the page

Assessment units and their categories: CGWB divides India into thousands of small units (blocks, mandals, talukas) and rates each Safe, Semi-Critical, Critical, Over-Exploited or Saline based on its stage of extraction; 'Over-Exploited' means extraction exceeds recharge

Recharge vs extractable resource vs extraction: annual recharge is the water nature returns to the aquifer each year, the extractable resource is the share of that which can be drawn, and extraction is what is actually pumped; the stage of extraction is the last divided by the second

Per-capita water availability and the Falkenmark thresholds: total renewable water divided by population, in cubic metres per person per year; below 1,700 is 'water-stressed' and below 1,000 is 'water-scarce'; a falling figure is driven as much by a growing population as by less water

Total resource vs utilizable water: most of India's average annual water resource cannot be captured and used; only the utilizable share (surface water that can be stored plus replenishable groundwater) is available supply, so the two must never be conflated

Freshwater withdrawal by sector is the split of water use between agriculture, industry and households; for India it is a snapshot carried forward by FAO AQUASTAT, not an annual trend, so read it as 'latest available'

Water productivity: economic output (GDP) per cubic metre of freshwater withdrawn; a low figure means water flows to low-value, thirsty uses, and a rising figure can simply reflect an economy shifting toward services rather than farms using water better

Safely managed drinking water (WHO/UNICEF JMP) means water on premises, available when needed and free of contamination; it measures the service delivered to homes, not whether the underlying aquifer is sustainable, so access can rise while the resource falls

Jal Jeevan Mission tap coverage is self-reported 'connections provided', not independently audited as functional; the CAG has flagged gaps between connections counted and taps that actually deliver water, so treat the figure as reported coverage, not guaranteed delivery

Groundwater contamination shares are the percentage of tested sites exceeding a safe limit for nitrate, fluoride, arsenic or uranium; these cluster in known problem areas and 'parts of' a district means contamination is localised within it, not district-wide

Why the national average misleads: a country-wide stage of extraction near 60% looks safe only because most of India is fine; it averages together the calm east and south with a north-west grain belt pumping well over 100%, so the average hides rather than reveals the crisis

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The percentage of annual groundwater extraction compared to the amount that can be sustainably drawn each year. Above 100% means the aquifer is being permanently depleted.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: This is the core metric indicating whether groundwater use is sustainable or mining reserves.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: A widely used indicator: a country is 'water-stressed' below 1,700 cubic metres per person per year, and 'water-scarce' below 1,000.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: India's per-capita availability has crossed the stress line and is approaching scarcity.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: Small administrative areas (blocks, mandals, talukas) used by the Central Ground Water Board to evaluate groundwater status locally.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: National averages hide local crises; breaking the country into units reveals over‑exploited pockets.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The portion of total renewable water that can actually be captured and used, considering limits of storage and extraction.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: India's total water resource is often cited as 1,999 BCM, but only 1,137 BCM is utilizable; the difference matters for planning.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: Economic output (GDP) produced per unit of freshwater withdrawn. Higher values mean more value per drop.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: India earns little per drop compared to its peers, largely because water is tied up in low‑value agriculture.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: Drinking water that is on premises, available when needed, and free of contamination, as defined by WHO/UNICEF.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: It measures service quality, not source sustainability; access can rise while water resources decline.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: A government programme aiming to provide tap water connections to all rural households.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: Reported connections surged from 16.7% to 79.7%, but functionality audits show gaps.

plannedCharts.title: India keeps slipping down the water ladder
plannedCharts.unit: cubic metres per person per year
plannedCharts.subtitle: CWC Reassessment of Water Availability, 2019 · average annual per-capita water availability
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The simplest measure of stress: how much water there is to go round, per person, as the population keeps growing.

plannedCharts.title: How much of India's water can actually be used
plannedCharts.subtitle: CWC water-resource estimation · total resource vs usable surface and groundwater
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The headline 'India has 1,999 BCM of water' is misleading - most of it cannot be captured and used.

plannedCharts.title: Nationally, India pumps about 60% of what refills each year
plannedCharts.subtitle: CGWB Dynamic Ground Water Resource Assessment · national stage of extraction, 2020-2025
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The single number officials cite to say groundwater is 'under control' - and the one that hides the most.

plannedCharts.title: Most blocks are safe - but one in nine is over-exploited
plannedCharts.subtitle: CGWB 2025 assessment · 6,762 assessment units by category
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Breaking the country into thousands of small assessment units shows the damage the national average buries.

plannedCharts.title: The crisis has an address: the north-west
plannedCharts.subtitle: CGWB 2025 assessment · stage of groundwater extraction by state
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Put extraction on a map and the abstract 60% average resolves into a sharp regional emergency.

plannedCharts.title: A calm national line, three states in free fall
plannedCharts.subtitle: CGWB assessments 2020-2025 · stage of extraction, national vs the north-west belt
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The honest test of the 'groundwater is improving' story: hold the national line against the worst states.

plannedCharts.title: Where India's water actually goes
plannedCharts.subtitle: World Bank / FAO AQUASTAT · freshwater withdrawal by sector (latest available)
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Before blaming taps and showers, see who the big user really is.

plannedCharts.title: India earns very little per drop
plannedCharts.subtitle: World Bank · water productivity (GDP per cubic metre of freshwater withdrawn)
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Water stress is also an efficiency story: how much economic value India wrings from each unit of water.

plannedCharts.title: The water that is left is often unsafe
plannedCharts.unit: % of tested samples above the safe limit
plannedCharts.subtitle: CGWB Annual Ground Water Quality Report 2024 · 15,259 monitoring sites
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Depletion is only half the problem - what remains is increasingly contaminated.

plannedCharts.title: Contamination reaches into hundreds of districts
plannedCharts.subtitle: CGWB 2024 report (Year-2023 data) · districts with groundwater contamination
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Quality problems are not a few isolated villages - they are spread across much of the country.

plannedCharts.title: Tap water reached most of rural India in five years
plannedCharts.subtitle: Jal Jeevan Mission · rural households with a tap-water connection
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The state's biggest recent water success, and the human counterpoint to the depletion story.

plannedCharts.title: Safe drinking water finally reaches most homes
plannedCharts.subtitle: World Bank / WHO-UNICEF JMP · population using safely managed drinking water
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The genuine good-news counterpoint: access has improved markedly.

plannedCharts.title: More taps, less water: the paradox in one frame
plannedCharts.subtitle: World Bank · drinking-water access vs renewable freshwater per person
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The article's thesis: India is getting better at delivering water to people while the resource itself shrinks.

selectionRules: Start from the page question, not from the indicator name.
Choose the smallest set of visuals that explains scale, trend, structure, comparison, and caveat.
Prefer mobile-friendly charts: line charts with sparse ticks, horizontal bars, share strips, pyramids only when essential, and no dense tables.
Use one strong pull quote only when the evidence supports it with a number.
Add glossary blocks for technical terms that normal readers may not know.
caveats: Use only figures present in lockedNumbers or sourceSummaries.
If a related theme indicator is present, you may use it for context, but do not pretend it is the main answer.
If source coverage is thin, say so directly.
Do not compare states, districts, or cities unless the evidence packet contains those geographies.
forbiddenClaims: Do not infer causality from a trend unless the evidence explicitly supports it.
Do not cite a source that is not present in sourceSummaries.
